Wow, that was a blast from the past...

Spectre built about 122 (?) joysticks and sold them with ICBM Attack cartridges.

Anything after that, I don't have any knowledge of (we did not do the conversion to using
standard handles).

The controller was a Radio Shack bakelite project box that we put a phone keypad, real pinball
flipper buttons and a X-Y joystick in. (I hand cut every lid for the joystick bevel personally)

As to the version that was released to the public domain, it was the code that would work
universally. We only had 5 games shipped when we encountered the problem. We modified the
code and shipped out new cartridges.

As to artwork, I have just about all of it in my attic. And all the Arcadian newsletters. And
Cursors too. Not sure about "Astrobugs newsletters".

I have the Treasure Cove Box, cartridge, and instructions. (only one though)

I think you have everything we shipped for ICBM Attack.

Brett

6282:
I think I was just adding to what I had responded to earlier...

That when we shipped ICBM Attack, it was with any cardboard box we could find laying 
around. And that I have somewhere a picture of our first shipment ready to go out. It was
a pile of various cardboard boxes plied up in my bedroom...

Esoterica only distributed Treasure Cove (it was too hard to make more handles). So the
only box art is for Treasure Cove.

That I still have the 'artwork' (paper) for the graphics.

I don't think I have the source code any longer. I developed the games on a modified TRS-
80. It had the same CPU (Z-80) that the Bally had. We modified a TRS-80 Memory
expansion to 'map' a code space directly into a cartridge interface to the Bally. Meaning
that the TRS-80 Memory expansion was 'pretending' to be a cartridge. (Basically we had
implemented a dual port memory arrangement.)

What this allowed was to use the TRS-80's Z80 compiler (I wrote an include file that
mapped all the system calls, equates, and variables used by the system as text strings so
development was easier). Also, while a game was running, the TRS-80 could examine and
change memory (variables could be read and modified in real-time).

A full 'compile' cycle consisted of compiling the Z-80 code, saving the object code to the
Expansion Memory, hitting reset on the Bally Arcade (this so it would read the new code it
thought was a cartridge), playing the game while watching what was going on from the
TRS-80.

In my opinion, this beat the crap out of the "ZGRASS" development systems being used by
Bally. The ZGRASS Arcade development systems were Fourth based beasts that were
impossible to program. I had one for a while when Action Graphics tried to get me to work
on a cartridge.

The ZGRASS system had so much overhead, it was a dog. Our TRS-80 system was simple,
machine code efficient, and allowed me to do both 3 tone music and 256 color graphics
(well, at least for the 'splash screen' of Treasure Cove and ICBM Attack. (I got the 256
colors working first, for ICBM Attack, then added the music when I did Treasure Cove.

I wrote the 3 tone music player, but George Moses was the guy that created most of the
music for it. I 'transcribed' one or two songs, but got bored pretty quick. I'm not a
musician, sorry.

I did create an ASDR engine for the Treasure Cove game (I was fascinated with exploring
what I could do with the hardware). An ASDR engine is the sound effects engine that
played the the bell clanging. ASDR stands for Attack Sustain Decay Release.
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADSR_envelope

But I digress...

Feel free to ask questions, I'll try to answer what I know (or can remember).

forward to hook up. The joystick just uses the potentiometers from two handles to provide
the X and Y control. The keypad is just a contact matrix using the up, down, left, and right

Great! So, I have good and bad news:
Good:
This means these recordings are encoded using Kansas City standard, 300-baud, 8 data bits, 2 stop bits, no parity.

Bad:
Although this is a well documented encoding format, I had trouble finding a program able to deal with "raw" data, most programs dealing with it expect the data is encoded in a given computer platform standard (e.g. Acorn Basic)

Good:
I found such a program:
http://www.netbay.com.au/~dxforth/kcs08.zip

Bad:
It is a MS-DOS program, and is going to be obsolete not far from now (Windows Vista 64 bit doesn't support DOS programs already)

Good:
The source code seems to be included!

Bad:
The source code is Forth-94!


This program I mentioned above seems to be somewhat "picky", I was unable to read "Mouse In The Hat (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud raw)(PD)[From Master Tapes].wav" using it, for instance. It only accepts 8-bit, 22050 kHz wave files as input (I converted the files accordingly for experimentation).

It converts wave files to binary and binary back to wave. For converting .wav to binary, the process is automatic (no parameters needed other than file name). For the last (successful) attempt to convert it back to wave, I used the following parameters:

-M, for generating a wav from a .prg file (the binary dump I generated before using the program);

I had some trouble with these phase distortions while trying to make my own programs for decoding the wave files. For reading digital data back from the tape, the loading program expects recorded pulses to have a precise length (given a certain threshold), in order to differentiate between 0 and 1 frequencies. Ah, I know why that is.  Many WaveMakers tapes came with both 300 and 2000 baud versions on the same tapes.  Sometimes, they'd put a 2000 baud program between loads of the 300 baud program!  So it would be arranged like:  intro to 300 baud program, 2000 baud program, main 300 baud program.  You'd tell Bally BASIC to load the program and start the recording from the beginning.  It would load the intro and start playing an introductory animation.  While this was playing, the 2000 baud program would play, but be ignored.  When the introduction was finished, it would tell Bally BASIC to start loading again.  At this point, the main 300 baud program would come up on the tape.

You can silence the 2000 baud portion (which sounds like a modem hiss rather than the more distinguishable 300 baud beeps) without any loss of data.  However, you can see from this example that accurately reproducting the timing of the original recordings--both the data rate and the length of any gaps--is important.

6415:
Naught to do with "Bank Switching" but how the AstroBASIC cartridge does
its tape interface without access to any I/O control lines ...

It's not voo-doo, well maybe a bit.  A write to any address between
14336 through 15359 will set a flip-flop to send a little voltage to the
line-input of the tape recorder, and a write to anywhere from 15360 to
16383 will reset the flip-flop and shut off the voltage.  Beyond that
it's just a matter of timing multiple pulses.
Reading an address in the 2K range of 14336 thru 16383 while playing
back that recording will result in the instantaneous voltage (or lack
thereof) from the tape showing up as a 1 or 0 on Data bit 0 - and
repeated readings by Astro Basic will result in re-creating the original
data stream.

This has nothing to do with hardware scaling. I thought the
question here was based on using the expander for characters
in a possible Venture, saving memory in ROM.

Enlarge is the wrong term first of all....you are looking
for Expand.

First read the magic register description......

MAGIC REGISTER
--------------
As described earlier, the Magic System is enabled when data is written
to a memory location (X) from 0 to 16K. A modified form of the data is
actually written in memory location X+16K. The magic register (output
port CH) determines how the data is modified. The purpose of each bit
of the magic register is shown below.
Bit 0 LSB of shift amount
1 MSB of shift amount
2 Rotate
3 Expand  <---------------------------
4 OR
5 XOR
6 Flop
The order in which magic functions are performed is as follows:
Expansion is done first; rotating or shifting; flopping; OR or XOR.
As many as four can be used at any one time and any function can be
bypassed. Rotate and shift as well as OR and XOR cannot be done at
the same time.


And read the description for the expand register

EXPAND
------
The expander is used to expand the 8 bit data bus into 8 pixels (or
16 bits). It expands a 0 on the data bus into a two-bit pixel and a
1 into another two-bit pixel. Thus, two-color patterns can be stored
in ROM in half the normal memory space.
During each memory write instruction using the expander, either the
upper half or the lower half of the data bus is expanded. The half
used is determined by the expand flip-flop. The flip-flop is reset by
an output to the magic register and is toggled after each magic memory
write. The upper half of the data bus is expanded when the flip-flop
is 0, and the lower half when the flip-flop is 1.
The expand register (output port 19H) determines the pixel values
into which the data bus will be expanded. A 0 on the data bus will be
expanded into the pixel defined by bits 0 and 1 of the expand
register.
A 1 on the data bus will be expanded into the pixel defined by bits
2 and 3 of the expand register.
The pixels generated by bit 0 or 4 of the data bus will be the least
significant pixel of the expanded byte. The most significant pixel
will come from bit 3 or 7.

As you can see, expansion is done in hardware and is part of
the magic function.
